digest.top_line: STELLAR: 3yr DFS 64.5% vs 62.3% (HR 0.883, NI P<.001) with LRR 8.4% vs 11.0% — 25 Gy/5fx TNT holds locoregional control against 50/25 chemoRT.
digest.tldr: Two Chinese phase III LARC trials move the RT question in opposite directions: STELLAR shortens RT to 5x5 with no LRR cost (8.4% vs 11.0%), while TNTCRT keeps LCRT unchanged in both arms and buys DFS purely through distant control (MFS HR 0.655, locoregional failure flat at 6.0% vs 6.2%). Lower GI carried the day; prostate was PSMA-PET methodology, not practice.

sites.intro: Both prostate items are PSMA-PET measurement questions, not treatment trials: what a PET finding means in BCR after salvage RT, and whether post-ARSI uptake change can be read as response at all.

studies.name: PSMA-Positive BCR Natural History Study
studies.tldr: Baseline of first 130 pts: most BCR men with PSADT >9-12mo still have PSMA-PET findings once PSA >5, mostly nodal.
details: 🔍 Prospective NCI natural-history cohort, PSMA-PET serial imaging, no mandated therapy; baseline data on first 130 pts
🔍 Eligibility: BCR after definitive therapy, PSA ≥0.5, all had salvage RT or declined it
🔍 Imaging schedule: baseline PET; negative → annual, any finding (incl. equivocal) → q6mo
📊 Vast majority of pts with PSADT >9mo and >12mo had PSMA-PET findings when PSA above 5
📊 Findings described as nodal disease, occasional small equivocal bone lesions, and prostate-bed recurrence
💊 Only about a third of pts have gone on therapy; majority observed off treatment
💊 Permitted therapy is short-course only (<6 months): intermittent ADT, SBRT, intermittent ARPI or Radium-223 trials
📊 Companion cohort (Madan, ~1.5yr f/u, first ~150 pts): 5 pts progressed on conventional imaging
⚠️ Numbers are investigator-stated in a video interview, not a peer-reviewed report; no CIs, denominators, or per-stratum counts given
⚠️ Single-center NCI referral cohort; PSA ≥0.5 floor and salvage-RT-exhausted requirement select against the lowest-volume BCR seen in community practice
⚠️ Cross-sectional baseline read only; median f/u ~2yr, longitudinal PET evolution data not yet reported

verdict.rationale: Baseline cross-section of an ongoing single-institution observational cohort, n=130, no comparator, no outcome data yet; investigator-reported percentages only.
verdict.audience: PSMA-PET-positive BCR post-definitive therapy, PSA ≥0.5, salvage RT given or declined

studies.significance: The RT-relevant read is that PSMA positivity is near-ubiquitous once PSA exceeds 5, even at PSADT >12mo, so a positive scan alone does not identify who needs metastasis-directed SBRT. Prostate-bed recurrence appears in a salvage-RT-exhausted cohort, which gates re-irradiation and nodal-field decisions.
studies.monday_clinic: In post-salvage-RT BCR with slow PSADT and a PSA above 5, this argues PSMA positivity alone is a weak trigger for metastasis-directed therapy; it says nothing about pts with rapid PSADT or PSA below 0.5, where the cohort has little data.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective observational natural-history cohort at the NCI with **serial PSMA PET** and no mandated treatment. Baseline analysis of the **first 130 pts** presented at GU ASCO 2026; the study is ongoing at a **median follow-up of about two years**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Biochemical recurrence after definitive therapy with **PSA ≥0.5** required for eligibility. All had **already received salvage radiation or declined it**, so this is a post-salvage population rather than first-recurrence.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: RT is not an intervention here; salvage RT is an **entry condition**. On-study **SBRT is permitted** under the general rule that any therapy lasting under six months is allowed. No dose, fractionation, or target-volume detail is reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: The presented analysis is a single-timepoint correlation of **PSMA PET findings against PSA doubling time**, the field's working predictor of metastasis in BCR. Longitudinal endpoints (imaging evolution, conventional-imaging progression) are stated as **not yet analyzed**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Among slow-doubling pts (**PSADT >9mo and >12mo**) the **vast majority had PSMA PET findings** once PSA was above 5, chiefly nodal, with prostate-bed recurrence and small equivocal bone lesions also described. **About one third** of pts have started any therapy. No per-stratum counts or confidence intervals are reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents PSMA-PET-positive BCR after definitive therapy and salvage RT, PSA ≥0.5, managed at a tertiary referral center. Does not represent conventional-imaging metastatic disease, hormone-sensitive de novo M1, or PSA levels below the 0.5 eligibility floor.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The cohort deliberately occupies the space EMBARK and the mCSPC trials do not: it was designed pre-EMBARK, and these pts would have been **ineligible for metastatic trials** because their disease was invisible on conventional imaging. Where oligometastasis trials such as STOMP and ORIOLE ask what to do with PSMA-detected lesions, this asks the prior question of how often they are there at all.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The source is a conference-interview transcript, so effect sizes arrive as **investigator description rather than tabulated data**: no denominators per doubling-time stratum, no CIs. The PSA ≥0.5 floor and salvage-RT-exhausted entry criterion make the detection rate an **upper bound** for a general BCR clinic.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The finding that PSMA positivity tracks PSA level more than doubling time **decouples imaging burden from prognosis**, which is the opposite of how a positive scan is often read. It does not establish that observation is safe; the follow-up analysis that would test that is still pending.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this cohort is not the detection rate itself but what the detection rate does to the interpretive weight of a positive scan. The field has largely absorbed PSMA PET as a staging upgrade: a scan turns positive, the patient is relabeled metastatic, and the treatment framework shifts from biochemical recurrence toward mCSPC intensification. The baseline data here undercut that reflex from the direction of prevalence. If men with doubling times over nine and over twelve months, the exact group historical BCR series identified as low risk, mostly have PSMA findings once PSA is above 5, then positivity is close to uninformative within that PSA range. A test that is positive in nearly everyone in a stratum cannot discriminate within that stratum, and the discrimination is what would justify escalating therapy.

The methodological caveats push in a specific direction rather than simply weakening the claim. The PSA floor of 0.5 and the requirement that salvage radiation was given or declined both select toward higher disease burden than a general biochemical-recurrence clinic, so the reported detection rate should be read as an upper bound. That matters because it does not rescue the discriminative argument: making the population less selected lowers positivity overall but does not obviously restore a correlation with doubling time. The more fragile part of the read is that the numbers arrive as investigator description in a conference interview rather than as a table, with no per-stratum denominators and no confidence intervals. Anyone using this to argue against treating a specific patient is leaning on a qualitative statement, not a published estimate.

For a radiation oncologist the practical content sits in two places the headline skips. First, prostate-bed recurrence is described in a cohort that has already exhausted salvage radiation, which raises the re-irradiation and nodal-field question rather than the metastasis-directed one, and the source gives no dose or target-volume detail to work from. Second, on-study therapy is capped at six months, so SBRT enters as a short-course intervention alongside intermittent systemic therapy rather than as a definitive alternative. That design choice means the cohort will eventually describe what happens when metastasis-directed treatment is used sparingly, which is a different question from the one STOMP and ORIOLE addressed.

What would have to be true for the reassuring read to be wrong is that the small equivocal bone lesions the investigators describe as uncertain turn out to behave like early metastases, in which case a substantial fraction of the observed group is accruing untreated disease that a positive scan correctly flagged. The companion analysis reporting five conventional-imaging progressions among roughly the first 150 patients at about eighteen months is consistent with indolence, but the follow-up is short relative to the multi-year natural history of biochemical recurrence, and a low event count at that interval is what an indolent cohort and a slowly declaring one look like alike. The interim longitudinal analysis the investigators describe as pending, not this baseline cross-section, is what will settle whether serial imaging adds anything over serial PSA.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Prostate-bed recurrence shows up in a cohort that has already had salvage RT, so the decision this touches is re-irradiation and nodal coverage, not first salvage. Near-universal PSMA positivity above PSA 5 means a positive scan alone is a weak trigger for metastasis-directed SBRT. No dose or target-volume detail in source.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Roughly a third of pts started any therapy and the rest are observed, with permitted treatment capped at six months, so this cohort tests whether intermittent or deferred systemic therapy is viable in PSMA-positive BCR. It argues against reflexively applying doublet or triplet mCSPC regimens to scan-detected disease.

open_questions: Does serial PSMA PET add prognostic value over serial PSA
Are small equivocal bone lesions true early metastases
Which PSMA-positive BCR pts can safely defer therapy

studies.name: PSMA PET Response Assessment Debate (USPCC)
studies.tldr: Uptake change after ARSI is prognostic (HR 5.03 for δ-percent SUVmax, n=16) but not a validated response measure; AR signaling drives PSMA expression.
details: 🔍 Position talk: PSMA uptake is androgen-receptor regulated, so post-therapy change may not track tumor burden
🔍 Cited series imaged pts immediately before and 2-4 mo after starting abiraterone or enzalutamide

details.text: 📊 Outcomes by δ-SUVmax response pattern (cited prospective series, 16 evaluable)
📐 Survival hazard ratios, wide intervals at n=16

subdetails: Median time to therapy change 9.6 mo (95% CI 6.9-14.2)

details: 📊 BAT: 3 of 6 men progressed on PSMA PET at 3 mo, before conventional imaging
🔍 RECIP 1.0 combines PSMA PET with CT to categorise PD, PR, SD, CR after radioligand therapy
⚠️ Repeatability work flags lesion identification and segmentation variability across serial SUVmax, SUVmean, SUVtotal, volume
⚠️ Evidence base is 16 and 6 pts, single-arm, no independent validation cohort

verdict.rationale: Point-counterpoint position talk, not a new result: its output is a recommendation against current use, supported by cited series of 16 and 6 pts.
verdict.audience: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer on abiraterone or enzalutamide

studies.significance: The reading that transfers: uptake change here is prognostic, not a burden measure. High δ-percent SUVmax carried median OS 17.8 vs 37.2 mo (HR 5.03, 95% CI 1.17-21.65) at n=16. For metastasis-directed planning, a PSMA PET obtained 2-4 months after ARSI or ADT start cannot be read as new disease without corroboration.
studies.monday_clinic: In a man restaged on PSMA PET 2-4 months after starting abiraterone or enzalutamide, this evidence context argues against calling rising uptake progression; it does not extend to staging in treatment-naive disease or to lesion detection, where the modality is not in dispute.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Point-counterpoint presentation**, not a new dataset. Reviews a prospective single-arm 18F-DCFPyL PET/CT series (**16 evaluable pts**), a 6-man bipolar androgen therapy imaging series, repeatability analyses, and the RECIP 1.0 framework.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: The cited series enrolled **metastatic androgen pathway modulation resistant** disease starting **abiraterone or enzalutamide**, imaged immediately before therapy and **2-4 months later**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Cited series reported **time to therapy change** and **overall survival**, stratified by δ-percent SUVmax (DPSM) and δ-absolute SUVmax (DASM). There is no prospective response-criterion validation endpoint anywhere in the talk.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: **RECIP 1.0** is the closest existing standard, built for **radioligand therapy** response, where the drug targets PSMA but does not manipulate the androgen axis. Nothing equivalent exists for scoring response during androgen-targeted therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents interpretation of serial PSMA PET during androgen axis-targeted therapy in metastatic castration-resistant disease. Does not represent staging or lesion detection, where PSMA PET performance is not the question here.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The **2-4 month imaging window** straddles uptake kinetics the talk itself calls uncharacterised, so scan timing and biology are confounded. Repeatability analyses show lesion identification and segmentation vary between acquisitions, and any δ-SUV threshold inherits that error.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The same series used to argue against response assessment shows **HR 5.03** and **HR 9.31** for survival, so the claim is not that the images carry no information. It is that **group-level prognostic separation at n=16 does not license an individual-patient response call**.

studies.interpretation:
The mechanistic claim is the strongest part of this position, and it is the part that generalises beyond the small series cited. If PSMA expression is regulated by androgen receptor signaling rather than fixed to tumor burden, then a PSMA PET obtained after starting an AR pathway inhibitor is reading two things at once: how much cancer is left, and how hard the drug is pushing on the receptor. Most imaging response biomarkers do not carry that property, because the tracer is not the therapy's own target. That is why the usual instinct, scoring a rising SUVmax as progression, is not safe here in the way it is for a size-based criterion.

The paradox in the talk is that the same prospective series used to argue against response assessment shows strong prognostic separation. High δ-percent SUVmax carried a hazard ratio of 5.03 (95% CI 1.17-21.65) and high δ-absolute SUVmax 9.31 (1.81-47.87), with median overall survival splitting 37.2 vs 17.8 months. Those are large numbers, and they come from 16 evaluable patients. An interval running from 1.17 to 21.65 is compatible with a modest effect and with an implausible one. Group-level prognostic separation and a usable response criterion at an individual decision point are different bars, and the second is the one being argued has not been cleared.

The repeatability data matter more than they usually would. A threshold-based criterion inherits the measurement error of the quantity it thresholds, so if lesion identification and segmentation vary between repeat acquisitions in the same patient, a δ-SUV cutoff is partly measuring the reader and the software. Add the 2 to 4 month imaging window used in the cited series and a second problem appears: the closing take-home is that the kinetics of androgen-driven PSMA change are not characterised, so a scan placed anywhere inside a two-month window may be sampling a moving pharmacodynamic curve rather than a stable disease state. Part of the observed split could be scan timing.

RECIP 1.0 is the strongest counterargument available, and its limits are worth stating plainly. It was built for radioligand therapy, where the treatment is directed at PSMA but is not an androgen axis manipulation, so its validation does not transfer automatically to scoring response during abiraterone, enzalutamide, or bipolar androgen therapy. The bipolar androgen therapy series shows the difficulty: three of six men progressed on PSMA PET before conventional imaging, which reads as a win for the modality, except that the intervention itself moves the androgen axis and the source does not state which way that pushes tracer uptake. Earlier detection and pharmacodynamic upregulation are not separable in six patients.

What this changes is scan reading, not treatment. A restaging PSMA PET taken in the months after androgen-targeted therapy starts should not be scored as burden change on its own, and a new or hotter lesion in that window needs corroboration before it drives a line switch or a metastasis-directed plan. What would have to change for the position to fail is specific and achievable: a characterised uptake time course, a fixed imaging interval, and reproducible automated segmentation, at which point prespecified δ-SUV thresholds become testable rather than post hoc.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Target selection is the exposed decision: a scan taken 2-4 months after ARSI or ADT start may show uptake shifts driven by AR signaling rather than new disease, so a fresh lesion in that window is thin grounds for adding an SBRT target. RECIP 1.0 was built for radioligand therapy response, and the source offers no criterion for post-RT scans.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Switching decisions carry the exposure: high δ-percent SUVmax tracked median time to therapy change 6.5 vs 12.2 mo, so rising uptake on a post-ARSI scan is group-level prognostic information, not evidence of progression in one patient. Bipolar androgen therapy adds the same confound, with six men imaged.

Whether RECIP 1.0 validates outside radioligand therapy

sites.intro: Two TNT phase IIIs that agree the added chemo works on distant failure and disagree only on how much RT you need to hold the pelvis.

studies.name: STELLAR
studies.tldr: 3yr DFS 64.5% vs 62.3%, HR 0.883, noninferior: 5x5 Gy then CAPOX matches long-course CRT in LARC.
details: 🔍 Open-label phase III, N=599, 16 Chinese centres, distal/middle-third cT3-4 and/or N+; median f/u 35.0 mo
🔍 RT: TNT arm 25 Gy/5fx then 4 cycles CAPOX; CRT arm 50 Gy/25fx with concurrent capecitabine; TME 6-8 wks after preop treatment
🔍 All pts got IMRT in both arms, CTV covered mesorectum, presacral space, internal iliac, obturator and ischiorectal fossa; external iliacs only for cT4b
📊 LRR was low and statistically indistinguishable, so shortening RT to 25 Gy/5fx cost nothing in locoregional control
📊 pCR + sustained cCR 21.8% TNT vs 12.3% CRT (P=.002); 9.4% vs 3.4% went to nonoperative management
⚠️ Acute grade III-V toxicity during preop treatment 26.5% vs 12.6% (P<.001), driven by haematologic G3-4 15.8% vs 2.0%
⚠️ OS gain sits on a secondary endpoint with no subgroup consistency, and Polish II's early OS advantage vanished by 8 years
⚠️ Preop completion was worse in TNT: 82.6% vs 95.2% any-dose, 74.8% vs 93.2% full-dose (both P<.001)
🔗 3yr LRR 8.4% / 11.0% sits with RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23 (4%-8.3%) and well below Polish II (21%-22%)
🔗 Unlike RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23, no 3yr DM reduction here (22.8% vs 24.7%), matching Polish II

verdict.rationale: Prespecified noninferiority met in a randomised phase III; supports an already guideline-listed TNT option. OS gain is secondary, unadjusted for multiplicity, follow-up only 35 mo.
verdict.audience: Distal/middle-third rectal adenocarcinoma, cT3-4 and/or node-positive, ECOG 0-1

studies.significance: Every pt received IMRT with a defined CTV (mesorectum, presacral, internal iliac, obturator, ischiorectal fossa; external iliacs only cT4b), the first of these TNT trials to do so, and 3yr LRR was 8.4% vs 11.0%. Compressing RT to 25 Gy/5fx did not cost locoregional control, which is the decision this moves.
studies.monday_clinic: In cT3-4 or node-positive middle or low rectal cancer heading for TME, this supports 25 Gy/5fx followed by CAPOX as an alternative to 50 Gy/25fx chemoRT; it does not speak to upper-third tumours, which were not enrolled.

primary_endpoint.name: 3-year disease-free survival
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: HR 0.883, one-sided 95% CI to 1.11, P<.001 for noninferiority

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multicenter **open-label randomised phase III**, 1:1, 16 hospitals across 11 Chinese provinces, enrolled Aug 2015 to Aug 2018. **N=599** (TNT 302, CRT 297), stratified by location, clinical stage and MRF status. Median follow-up **35.0 months**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Age 18-70, ECOG 0-1, **cT3-4 and/or node-positive** rectal adenocarcinoma of the distal or middle third, no distant metastases and no prior anticancer treatment. Baseline was balanced: cT4 15.9% v 12.8%, MRF involvement 56.3% v 56.2%, and staging was by central MRI read independently by three radiologists.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: TNT arm **25 Gy in 5 fractions**, then CAPOX starting 7-14 days later; CRT arm **50 Gy in 25 fractions** with concurrent capecitabine 825 mg/m2 bid. **All pts received IMRT**, with CTV covering mesorectum, presacral space, internal iliac, obturator nodes and ischiorectal fossa (external iliacs only if cT4b), superior border at the sacral promontory, inferior 2-3 cm below the tumour, CTV to PTV 0.5-1.0 cm. Plans went through central QA.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: TNT: **4 cycles preop CAPOX** (oxaliplatin 130 mg/m2 d1, capecitabine 1,000 mg/m2 bid d1-14) plus 2 postop cycles. CRT: concurrent capecitabine then **6 postop CAPOX cycles**. TME at 6-8 weeks, with watch-and-wait permitted for cCR.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: 3-year DFS**, noninferiority margin **HR 1.43** (equivalently an 11% absolute margin against an assumed 65% CRT rate), one-sided alpha 0.05, ≥194 events for ≥80% power. Secondary: OS, MFS, LRR, surgical complications, toxicity and completion rates.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Noninferiority met: the 95% upper bound of **1.11** sat below the 1.43 margin. R0 resection 91.5% v 87.8% (P=.189); combined pCR plus sustained cCR **21.8% v 12.3% (P=.002)**, and 28 TNT pts (9.4%) v 10 CRT (3.4%) avoided surgery entirely.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Preop grade III-V toxicity **26.5% v 12.6% (P<.001)**, almost entirely haematologic (G3-4 **15.8% v 2.0%**) plus thrombocytopenia 11.1% v 0.7%. Grade III+ surgical complications were similar (14.0% v 15.7%, P=.625) with no 30-day postoperative deaths. **Late toxicity and QoL are not reported here.**

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The 3yr LRR of 8.4% and 11.0% matches RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23 (**4%-8.3%**) and is far below Polish II (**21%-22%**), which enrolled fixed cT3/cT4 disease. Unlike RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23, STELLAR showed **no 3yr DM reduction** (22.8% v 24.7%), tracking Polish II instead. Preop grade 3+ toxicity (26.5%) was lower than the ~47% seen with FOLFIRINOX in PRODIGE 23.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents middle and low rectal adenocarcinoma, cT3-4 or node-positive, ECOG 0-1, age ≤70, treated with IMRT and TME. Does not represent upper-third tumours, age >70, unresectable fixed cT4 disease of the Polish II type, or anyone needing a late-toxicity or QoL comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The OS difference is a secondary endpoint tested two-sided without multiplicity control, and subgroup analysis showed no consistent OS effect. Deaths in the interval before surgery ran 3 per arm and 53 pts refused surgery without cCR (17 TNT, 36 CRT), an imbalance that touches the arms unevenly. The authors concede the NI margin was wide in retrospect.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The trial answers a logistics question as much as an efficacy one: one week of RT plus chemotherapy delivered when pts can still tolerate it, versus five weeks of chemoRT and adjuvant chemotherapy most pts do not finish. The tradeoff is front-loaded haematologic toxicity. What it does not settle is whether the OS separation is real.

studies.interpretation:
STELLAR is the third randomised trial to put short-course radiotherapy plus neoadjuvant chemotherapy against long-course chemoradiation, and its value lies less in the primary endpoint than in what surrounds it. Noninferiority on 3-year DFS was met, but with a margin of HR 1.43 that the authors themselves call wide in retrospect. An 11% absolute allowance is generous, and a trial designed to a narrower margin would have needed a larger sample. Read strictly, the DFS result licenses the schedule rather than establishing equivalence.

The locoregional data carry more weight for a radiation oncologist than the survival curves do. Three-year LRR was 8.4% with 25 Gy in 5 fractions and 11.0% with 50 Gy in 25, and the difference is well inside noise. That number is the one to take forward, because STELLAR is the only one of these trials in which every pt received IMRT, with a defined CTV and central plan QA. Polish II reported 21%-22% LRR, but it enrolled fixed cT3 and cT4 disease and predates routine IMRT, so the comparison says as much about population and technique as about fractionation. RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23 sit at 4%-8.3%, where STELLAR also sits. The consistent read across all four is that hypofractionation does not cost local control in MRI-staged, adequately treated disease, and STELLAR is the cleanest technical demonstration of it.

The OS finding, 86.5% versus 75.1% with HR 0.67, is the part that should move confidence least. It is secondary, tested two-sided without multiplicity adjustment, and the subgroup analysis showed no consistent direction. More instructive is the precedent the authors name themselves: Polish II saw the same early OS advantage and lost it by 8 years. There is no mechanistic account of how a shorter RT course with the same total systemic exposure would improve survival while leaving MFS and LRR untouched, and 22.8% versus 24.7% distant metastasis argues the same way. Absent a mechanism through which the arms diverge, the most economical explanation is that 35 months of follow-up caught a fluctuation in a control arm that fared worse than the assumed 65% DFS.

What is durable, and what will not appear in a subgroup table, is compliance. Only 74.8% of TNT pts completed preoperative treatment at full dose against 93.2% in the CRT arm, so the front-loading is not free. But 60.0% versus 48.3% completed planned adjuvant cycles, and combined pCR plus sustained cCR reached 21.8% versus 12.3%, with 9.4% versus 3.4% of pts avoiding surgery altogether. In a low rectal tumour where the alternative is an abdominoperineal resection, that gap is arguably the most clinically consequential number in the paper, and it is not what the trial was designed to measure.

The cost is real and lands on the medical oncologist: grade 3-4 haematologic toxicity of 15.8% against 2.0%, moving four cycles of CAPOX ahead of surgery. That is a manageable and predictable trade for a fit pt, less so for a marginal one, and the trial excluded anyone over 70. What would have to be true for this to be wrong is that the DFS margin masked a real detriment, or that longer follow-up reverses the direction as Polish II did. Neither would touch the local control conclusion, which is the one this trial actually earns.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: 25 Gy/5fx gave 3yr LRR 8.4% vs 11.0% for 50 Gy/25fx, and STELLAR is the only trial in this set where every pt got IMRT with a defined CTV (mesorectum, presacral, internal iliac, obturator, ischiorectal fossa) and central plan QA. That makes the fractionation result transferable, not technique-confounded.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Moving 4 cycles of CAPOX preoperatively raised planned-cycle completion to 60.0% vs 48.3%, but cost grade 3-4 haematologic toxicity of 15.8% vs 2.0% and dropped full-dose preop completion to 74.8% vs 93.2%. The sequencing gain is real; the front-loaded myelosuppression is the price.

studies.name: TNTCRT
studies.tldr: 3yr DFS 74.8% vs 66.0%, HR 0.674, P=.016 for doublet CAPOX TNT with LCRT vs standard nCRT in high-risk LARC.
details: 📊 MFS 77.7% v 67.6%, HR 0.655 (0.469-0.915) · the DFS gain is distant control, not local
📊 Locoregional failure flat: 6.03% v 6.19%, P=.943 · LCRT was identical in both arms
📊 3yr OS 90.2% v 87.5%, P=.167 · no survival separation at 51mo median f/u
🔍 Phase III, N=458 (232 doublet-LC TNT v 226 nCRT), stage II/III LARC, ≥1 MRI high-risk feature (cT4a-b, cN2, MRF+, cT3c-d with EMVI), age 18-70
💊 Experimental: 1 cycle induction CAPOX → LCRT with 2 cycles concurrent CAPOX → 3 cycles consolidation CAPOX → TME. Control: LCRT + concurrent capecitabine → TME → 6 cycles adjuvant CAPOX
⚠️ Neoadjuvant-phase G3+ AEs 27.59% v 8.56%, P<.001; whole-course severe toxicity comparable (28.02% v 24.32%, P=.371)
⚠️ Both arms delivered LCRT, so this trial cannot speak to SCRT-based TNT (RAPIDO/STELLAR) or RT omission
⚠️ ~87% v ~90% went to TME · surgery rates not identical, and no watch-and-wait endpoint reported in source
🔗 vs RAPIDO/PRODIGE-23/STELLAR: those tested TNT vs nCRT with different RT or chemo scaffolds; TNTCRT isolates uninterrupted doublet chemo around an unchanged LCRT backbone

verdict.rationale: Phase III, prespecified DFS primary met, 51mo median follow-up. Aligns with RAPIDO/PRODIGE-23 TNT direction rather than contesting it; OS unchanged, age ≤70 only.
verdict.audience: High-risk stage II/III rectal, cT4/cN2/MRF+/EMVI, age 18-70

studies.significance: RT was constant across arms (LCRT both), so every bit of the DFS gain is chemotherapy intensification: locoregional failure sat at 6.03% v 6.19%. Nothing here licenses changing dose, target volume, or dropping RT. The decision it moves is chemo sequencing around an unchanged LCRT backbone, and pCR nearly tripled (26.37% v 9.80%), which matters if you are building toward organ preservation.
studies.monday_clinic: In a fit pt aged 70 or younger with MRI high-risk stage II/III rectal cancer (cT4, cN2, threatened MRF, or EMVI), this supports uninterrupted doublet chemo around long-course RT over standard nCRT with adjuvant chemo; it does not inform RT technique or extend above age 70.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multicenter, randomized, **phase III**, enrolling June 6 2017 to December 27 2023. **N=458** (232 doublet-LC TNT, 226 nCRT). Median follow-up **51 months**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Stage II/III LARC with **at least 1 MRI high-risk feature**: cT4a-b, cN2, mesorectal fascia involvement, or cT3c-d with extramural vascular invasion. Baseline burden was heavy: cT4 47.82%, cN2 75.98%, threatened MRF 70.96%, EMVI 54.80%. **Age capped at 70.**

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Experimental arm ran **uninterrupted CAPOX** across the whole neoadjuvant block: 1 induction cycle, 2 concurrent with RT, 3 consolidation, then surgery. Control took LCRT with **concurrent capecitabine alone**, surgery, then 6 cycles adjuvant CAPOX starting 4 to 8 weeks post-op.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Both arms received long-course RT**, so RT is the fixed backbone and not the variable under test. Dose, fractionation, and target volume are not reported in the source text.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: DFS.** Secondary reported here: MFS, pCR, locoregional failure, OS, neoadjuvant and whole-course grade ≥3 toxicity, major postoperative complications.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: The separation is distant, not local: MFS moved (HR 0.655) while locoregional failure was **flat at ~6% in both arms**. **OS 90.2% v 87.5%, P=.167**, immature at 51 months.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Grade ≥3 AEs during the neoadjuvant phase roughly tripled (**27.59% v 8.56%, P<.001**), but whole-course severe toxicity (28.02% v 24.32%, P=.371) and major postoperative complications (3.98% v 2.94%, P=.567) matched. Front-loading toxicity, not adding it.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RAPIDO and STELLAR paired TNT with **short-course RT**; PRODIGE-23 used induction FOLFIRINOX before LCRT. TNTCRT is the LCRT-plus-doublet-throughout permutation, and the authors say directly that comparison against SCRT-based and nondoublet-concurrent TNT regimens is still owed.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents high-risk stage II/III LARC aged 18 to 70 with MRI-defined adverse features. Does not represent pts over 70, low-risk cT3a-b node-negative disease, or anyone being considered for RT omission.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Locoregional failure was already near-floor at ~6%, so the trial had no room to demonstrate an RT-side effect even had one existed. Surgery rates differed slightly (~87% v ~90%) with no organ-preservation endpoint reported, and the ≤70 age cap leaves the group most likely to struggle with uninterrupted CAPOX untested.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: This settles regimen intensity within LCRT-based TNT, not the SCRT-versus-LCRT question that actually divides practice. With locoregional control saturated and OS flat, the case for the intensified arm rests on DFS and MFS, both driven by distant control, plus a pCR signal that is a means to organ preservation rather than an outcome in itself.

studies.interpretation:
The most useful way to read TNTCRT is by what it holds constant. Both arms got long-course radiotherapy, and both got the same drugs; what moved was when the oxaliplatin doublet was given and whether it ran without interruption. That design makes this a clean test of chemotherapy sequencing and intensity, and a test of nothing at all about radiotherapy. A radiation oncologist looking for permission to change dose, target volume, or fractionation will not find it here.

The result lands where the TNT literature already pointed. RAPIDO and STELLAR established that front-loading systemic therapy improves distant control, and PRODIGE-23 did the same with induction FOLFIRINOX before long-course chemoradiation. TNTCRT's HR of 0.674 for DFS is consistent with that body of work rather than a departure from it. What it adds is a specific permutation the earlier trials did not test: doublet chemotherapy running continuously through induction, concurrent, and consolidation phases around an unchanged LCRT backbone. The authors are candid that the comparison the field actually wants, this regimen against short-course-based and nondoublet-concurrent TNT, remains unrun.

The internal structure of the benefit is worth dwelling on. Metastasis-free survival moved with almost exactly the DFS hazard ratio while locoregional failure sat at 6.03% versus 6.19%. That is not a subtle finding; it means the entire DFS gain is distant disease control, and it means locoregional control was already at a floor that no amount of systemic intensification was going to lower. A skeptic could reasonably say that a trial in which one of the two components of the composite endpoint does not move at all is really a metastasis trial wearing a DFS label. That is not a criticism of the result, but it does define its reach.

Confidence should be tempered by two things. Overall survival did not separate (90.2% v 87.5%, P=.167), which at 51 months median follow-up is uninformative rather than negative, but it does mean the case rests on a surrogate. And the trial enrolled only patients aged 70 or younger. Uninterrupted CAPOX with a grade 3 or higher neoadjuvant event rate of 27.59% is precisely the regimen where an older, less fit population would be expected to diverge, through dose reductions, omitted consolidation cycles, and a diluted delivered intensity. Extrapolating this hazard ratio to a general clinic population would likely overstate it.

The toxicity picture is more favorable than the headline number suggests, and this is the part most likely to change a multidisciplinary discussion. Grade 3 or higher events tripled during the neoadjuvant phase but were comparable across the entire treatment course, and major postoperative complications were unchanged. That pattern says the regimen relocates toxicity to a window when patients are fittest and compliance is highest, rather than adding it. Adjuvant CAPOX after total mesorectal excision is notoriously underdelivered; moving it forward converts a planned dose into a received one.

What would have to be true for this to be wrong? Chiefly, that the DFS advantage narrows as follow-up matures, which has happened before in this setting when early distant control did not translate into durable benefit. Continued follow-up for long-term survival, late toxicity, and function is the right next read.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: LCRT was identical in both arms, so nothing here touches dose, fractionation, or target volume, and locoregional failure was already at floor (6.03% v 6.19%). The RT-relevant read is the pCR jump to 26.37% from 9.80%, which is the currency of watch-and-wait conversations. This trial does not inform SCRT versus LCRT.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The variable under test is yours: uninterrupted CAPOX through induction, concurrent, and consolidation versus concurrent capecitabine plus 6 cycles of post-op adjuvant CAPOX. DFS HR 0.674 with whole-course severe toxicity unchanged (28.02% v 24.32%) argues the benefit comes from delivering the doublet when pts can actually take it. Untested above age 70.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Surgery followed in roughly 87% v 90% of pts and major postoperative complications were comparable (3.98% v 2.94%, P=.567), so front-loading the doublet did not degrade the operation. The pCR rate near-tripling (26.37% v 9.80%) is the number that reshapes preoperative discussion, though no organ-preservation endpoint is reported in source.

papers.title: Total Neoadjuvant Therapy With Long-Course Radiotherapy Versus Chemoradiotherapy in High-Risk Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer (TNTCRT): A Multicenter, Randomized, Phase III Trial
papers.abstract: PURPOSE High-risk locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) carries a substantial risk of distant recurrence, which limits disease-free survival (DFS). We compared total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) integrating long-course radiotherapy (LCRT) with uninterrupted doublet chemotherapy (doublet-LC TNT) versus conventional neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT). METHODS In this multicenter, randomized, phase III trial, patients with stage II/III LARC and at least 1 high-risk feature (cT4a-b, cN2, mesorectal fascia involvement, or cT3c-d with extramural vascular invasion) were enrolled. Patients were assigned to doublet-LC TNT (induction, concurrent, and consolidation capecitabine plus oxaliplatin with LCRT) before surgery or nCRT (capecitabine with LCRT) followed by surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy. The primary end point was DFS (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03177382 ). RESULTS Between June 6, 2017, and December 27, 2023, 458 patients were randomly assigned to doublet-LC TNT (n = 232) or nCRT (n = 226). At a median follow-up of 51 months, doublet-LC TNT improved 3-year DFS (74.8% v 66.0%; hazard ratio [HR], 0.674 [95% CI, 0.489 to 0.929]; P = .016). Metastasis-free survival (MFS; 77.7% v 67.6%; HR, 0.655 [95% CI, 0.469 to 0.915]) and pathologic complete response rates (pCR; 26.37% v 9.80%; P < .001) were higher with doublet-LC TNT, whereas locoregional failure remained low and comparable (6.03% v 6.19%; P = .943). Although grade ≥3 adverse events during the neoadjuvant phase were more frequent with doublet-LC TNT (27.59% v 8.56%; P < .001), severe toxicities during the entire treatment course (28.02% v 24.32%; P = .371) and major postoperative complications (3.98% v 2.94%; P = .567) were comparable. CONCLUSION Compared with conventional nCRT, doublet-LC TNT improved DFS, MFS, and pCR rates with manageable toxicity. These findings support this intensified, doublet-based regimen as a standard option within the modern TNT paradigm. Further comparative studies are warranted to evaluate these results against other short-course radiotherapy‑based or nondoublet-concurrent TNT regimens.

papers.title: Multicenter, Randomized, Phase III Trial of Short-Term Radiotherapy Plus Chemotherapy Versus Long-Term Chemoradiotherapy in Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer (STELLAR)
papers.abstract: PURPOSE To ascertain if preoperative short-term radiotherapy followed by chemotherapy is not inferior to a standard schedule of long-term chemoradiotherapy in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer. MATERIALS AND METHODS Patients with distal or middle-third, clinical primary tumor stage 3-4 and/or regional lymph node–positive rectal cancer were randomly assigned (1:1) to short-term radiotherapy (25 Gy in five fractions over 1 week) followed by four cycles of chemotherapy (total neoadjuvant therapy [TNT]) or chemoradiotherapy (50 Gy in 25 fractions over 5 weeks, concurrently with capecitabine [chemoradiotherapy; CRT]). Total mesorectal excision was undertaken 6-8 weeks after preoperative treatment, with two additional cycles of CAPOX (intravenous oxaliplatin [130 mg/m 2 , once a day] on day 1 and capecitabine [1,000 mg/m 2 , twice a day] from days 1 to 14) in the TNT group and six cycles of CAPOX in the CRT group. The primary end point was 3-year disease-free survival (DFS). RESULTS Between August 2015 and August 2018, a total of 599 patients were randomly assigned to receive TNT (n = 302) or CRT (n = 297). At a median follow-up of 35.0 months, 3-year DFS was 64.5% and 62.3% in TNT and CRT groups, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.883; one-sided 95% CI, not applicable to 1.11; P < .001 for noninferiority). There was no significant difference in metastasis-free survival or locoregional recurrence, but the TNT group had better 3-year overall survival than the CRT group (86.5% v 75.1%; P = .033). Treatment effects on DFS and overall survival were similar regardless of prognostic factors. The prevalence of acute grade III-V toxicities during preoperative treatment was 26.5% in the TNT group versus 12.6% in the CRT group ( P < .001). CONCLUSION Short-term radiotherapy with preoperative chemotherapy followed by surgery was efficacious with acceptable toxicity and could be used as an alternative to CRT for locally advanced rectal cancer.
